newsitem.title: USA: "Oddfather" normal at home, New York jury is told.
newsitem.headline: "Oddfather" normal at home, New York jury is told.

text.p: FBI agents testified Thursday in the trial of Vincent "The Chin" Gigante that the accused mob boss, known for wandering city streets in a ragged bathrobe and mumbling, behaved normally at home.
Prosecutors say Gigante has feigned mental illness for years to avoid prosecution, but defence attorneys have argued he is incapable of understanding the charges against him.
The reputed head of the Genovese crime family faces a 21-count murder and racketeering indictment.

FBI agent Charles Beaudoin testified on the trial's second day that he watched Gigante at the New York home of his girlfriend from an adjacent apartment. He said Gigante wore street clothes as he held late-night meetings with other reputed organised crime figures.
Gigante has earned the nicknames "The Oddfather" and "The Robe" for wearing a dirty, ragged bathrobe while wandering around Greenwich Village and mumbling to himself.

The subject of Gigante's attire prompted Judge Jack Weinstein to order him Thursday to appear cleanshaven and in business attire, such as a blazer jacket, by Monday. He has appeared for the two days of his trial unshaven, in a blue windbreaker and baggy trousers, seated in a wheelchair.
"A blazer?" defence attorney Machael Marinaccio asked in response to the judge's order. "I don't think a blue blazer, tan pants and deck shoes are in the offing here, judge."

Defence attorney James Culleton hammered away at the FBI agent and other investigators who testified about their surveillance of Gigante. Under cross-examination, they conceded that while they could see him, they did not know what he was saying or doing.
The trial comes seven years after Gigante, 69, was first charged.

He is accused of ordering the murders of seven people and conspiring to kill three others. He allegedly ordered the murders to avenge breaches of organised crime protocol, including unauthorised slayings, prosecutors said.
Gigante has checked himself into hospitals dozens of times over the past 25 years in what authorities say was a strategy to avoid prosecution.
The trial is expected to last five weeks. Gigante is free on $1 million bail.
